claims.sentence: The NHS says most sore throats are caused by viruses such as colds or flu, and bacteria are a less common cause.
claims.evidence: Only a University Hospitals Sussex A&E leaflet text said sore throats are usually caused by viruses like colds or flu, less often bacteria; nhs.uk page text for this was not returned. NICE NG84 says acute sore throat is often caused by a viral infection.
claims.newSentence: NICE says acute sore throat is often caused by a viral infection, and most people get better without an antibiotic.

claims.sentence: Laryngitis, tonsillitis, strep throat and glandular fever can also cause a sore throat, and so can smoking.
claims.evidence: Sussex leaflet lists tonsillitis, laryngitis, strep throat and glandular fever as other frequent causes. Search said it found nothing on smoking as a cause.
claims.newSentence: A University Hospitals Sussex NHS leaflet lists tonsillitis, laryngitis, strep throat and glandular fever as other common causes of a sore throat.

claims.sentence: NICE says that in older children and adults, pus on the tonsils, painful glands in the neck and a fever without a cough point more towards a bacterial infection.
claims.evidence: NICE returned text: FeverPAIN or Centor criteria identify people more likely to benefit from an antibiotic; fever, pus on tonsils and no cough score points (FeverPAIN), tender neck glands is a Centor item; FeverPAIN 2-3 linked to 34-40% chance of streptococcus. 'Point more towards bacterial' and 'older children and adults' not shown.
claims.newSentence: NICE suggests scoring tools (FeverPAIN or Centor) to spot people with a sore throat who may be more likely to benefit from an antibiotic, and these include fever, pus on the tonsils, tender neck glands and no cough.

claims.sentence: A sore throat usually clears up on its own and often lasts about a week.
claims.evidence: NICE: acute sore throat often caused by a virus and lasts about a week; NHS sore throat page: normally gets better by itself within a week.

claims.sentence: Paracetamol or ibuprofen can help with pain and fever, although not everyone can take ibuprofen safely, so a pharmacist can advise.
claims.evidence: 111 Wales text: ask a pharmacist about paracetamol or ibuprofen for the pain; Sussex leaflet: not everyone can take ibuprofen safely. 'Fever' not in retrieved text; Cheshire page text not confirmed for this.
claims.newSentence: NHS 111 Wales says a pharmacist can advise about paracetamol or ibuprofen for the pain, and a hospital trust leaflet notes that not everyone can take ibuprofen safely.

claims.sentence: Drinking fluids and resting are also advised.
claims.evidence: No retrieved text mentioned fluids or rest.

claims.sentence: NICE says most people with a sore throat will not need an antibiotic.
claims.evidence: NICE: in most cases acute sore throat is self-limiting, often viral, and most people will not need an antibiotic.

claims.sentence: The NHS says antibiotics are prescribed only if the GP thinks a bacterial infection is likely.
claims.evidence: No retrieved nhs.uk text said this. What was retrieved: NICE says FeverPAIN or Centor should be used to identify people who may be more likely to benefit from an antibiotic.
claims.newSentence: NICE says a scoring tool (FeverPAIN or Centor) should be used to identify people with a sore throat who may be more likely to benefit from an antibiotic.

claims.sentence: Tonsillitis commonly causes a sore throat, trouble swallowing, fever, earache and tender swollen glands in the neck.
claims.evidence: Tonsillitis page text retrieved covered diagnosis, swab, blood test, quinsy and emergency signs, not the symptom list.

claims.sentence: A GP can usually diagnose tonsillitis from the symptoms and a look at the throat, and may arrange a swab or a glandular fever blood test if symptoms are severe or persistent.
claims.evidence: NHS tonsillitis: GP can often diagnose from symptoms and a look at the throat; a swab can show if bacteria are the cause; glandular fever blood test recommended if symptoms are severe or will not go away. The swab is not tied to severity.
claims.newSentence: A GP can often diagnose tonsillitis from the symptoms and a look at the throat, a swab can show whether bacteria are the cause, and a blood test for glandular fever is recommended if symptoms are severe or will not go away.

claims.sentence: Glandular fever can cause a high temperature, swollen glands, a sore throat, rash, headache and tiredness, and the NHS says it is most common in people aged 15 to 24.
claims.evidence: NHS glandular fever page: most common in people aged 15 to 24. The symptom list was not in retrieved text.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says glandular fever is most common in people aged 15 to 24.

claims.sentence: Antibiotics do not work for glandular fever because it is caused by a virus.
claims.evidence: NHS glandular fever: GP will not give antibiotics because it is viral and antibiotics do not work.

claims.sentence: Quinsy is a collection of pus between the tonsil and the wall of the throat, and is a rare complication of tonsillitis.
claims.evidence: NHS tonsillitis: quinsy is a pocket of pus (abscess) between the tonsil and the wall of the throat, a complication of tonsillitis. 'Rare' not shown.
claims.newSentence: Quinsy is a collection of pus between the tonsil and the wall of the throat, and is a complication of tonsillitis.

claims.sentence: Sources agree on seeking advice from a GP if the sore throat has not improved after a week, if there is a high temperature or the person feels hot and shivery, or if the immune system is weakened or a medicine could be causing the sore throat.
claims.evidence: NHS sore throat page: get an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for a very high temperature, feeling hot, cold or shivery, or a weakened immune system; NHS Inform: contact GP if not improved after a week. The sentence puts fever/immune weakness into a routine GP bucket (downgrades urgency). 'Medicine could be causing it' not found. 'Sources agree' not shown.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says to contact a GP practice if a sore throat has not started to improve after a week, and to ask for an urgent GP appointment or call NHS 111 for a very high temperature, feeling hot, cold or shivery, or a weakened immune system.

claims.sentence: A sore throat that does not get better within 10 to 14 days, or that gets worse rather than better, may suggest glandular fever.
claims.evidence: Cheshire and Merseyside NHS text: a sore throat that does not get better within 10 to 14 days or gets worse may suggest glandular fever. Attribution is to this page, not nhs.uk.

claims.sentence: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for struggling to breathe, being unable to swallow even with pain relief, or drooling or spitting out saliva because swallowing is too painful.
claims.evidence: NHS: call 999 or go to A&E for difficulty breathing or being unable to swallow, drooling, high-pitched sound when breathing, or severe symptoms getting worse quickly. 'Even with pain relief' and 'spitting out saliva' not shown.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for difficulty breathing, being unable to swallow, or drooling.

claims.sentence: Other reasons are a high-pitched noise when breathing in, a sore throat that is severe and getting worse quickly, swelling inside the mouth or throat, or trouble speaking.
claims.evidence: NHS sore throat: high-pitched breathing sound, severe symptoms getting worse quickly; NHS tonsillitis: swelling inside the mouth or throat, trouble speaking, swallowing or breathing. 999/A&E route matches.

claims.sentence: NHS 111 Wales advises that a person should not drive themselves to A&E but should ask someone to drive them or call 999.
claims.evidence: 111 Wales: if you need emergency help don't drive to A&E yourself; ask someone to drive you or call 999.

claims.sentence: Most sore throats are caused by viruses and clear up on their own, but struggling to breathe or swallow needs 999 or A&E.
claims.evidence: Consistent with NICE (often viral, most people get better without antibiotics) and NHS 999/A&E signs for breathing and swallowing difficulty.

notes: Searches were thin on nhs.uk text for several points (smoking, fluids/rest, tonsillitis symptom list, 'medicine causing sore throat'); these were not confirmed. c14 downgraded urgency for high temperature and weakened immune system (NHS: urgent GP appointment or 111). c16 and c17 should be merged-checked so the 999/A&E list is not duplicated. The 111 Wales URL for c17 and c05 text was not confirmed for every item. Several first-pass statements attributed to 'the NHS' came only from hospital or ICB leaflets. Mind consistency with the site's own sore throat symptom page if it gives different routes.
